history.content: How does the system classify the different types of issues?

The system classifies issues into two types: classifiers and collections. Classifiers can be text classifiers or document classifiers, which classify documents based on words and phrases extracted from the body text, taking into account part of speech information and other enrichments. Collections are sets of documents that can be enriched and later searched for meaningful information. Additionally, there are limitations and known issues related to IBM Watsonx.data, such as the inability for a user with certain access levels to view created schemas or run select queries, and the partial support for CREATE VIEW statements in Db2 and Netezza.
How do I create a text classifier?

To create a text classifier, follow these steps:
1. Open the Discovery user interface.
2. Add a classifier enrichment.
3. Provide the necessary training data in CSV format. This data should include natural language text along with their corresponding labels or class names.
4. Click on "Create."
5. Select the collection and field where you want to apply the text classifier enrichment, then click "Apply."
The text classifier will analyze the provided text and classify it based on the words and phrases, considering their part of speech information. 
For more information, please refer to the documentation on [Classifier](https://cloud.ibm.com/docs/discovery-data?topic=discovery-data-domain-classifier). The text classifier utilizes part of speech information, regardless of whether the part of speech enrichment is applied to the project.
What is the difference between a document classifier and a text classifier?

A document classifier can classify documents based on words and phrases extracted from the body text fields, taking into account part of speech information, other enrichments applied to the body text, and information from non-body fields. On the other hand, a text classifier classifies documents based on words and phrases extracted from the body text, considering their part of speech information. The main difference lies in the additional information used by the document classifier for classification.
For more information, you can refer to the provided document discussing the difference between a document classifier and a text classifier.

IBM Watson™ Discovery provides two levels of language support: Basic and Full. When you create a collection, you must specify its language, and all documents added to that collection must be written in the same language. Natural Language Understanding supports various languages, but the available features may differ by language. Currently, English is the only language supported across all features, while the other languages have limited support. IBM Watson® Language Translator supports a wide range of translatable languages and offers customization for many translation models.

IBM Watson® Discovery is an intelligent document processing engine designed to help you extract insights from complex business documents. With Discovery, you can visually train AI to deeply understand your content, including tables and images, enabling you to uncover hidden business value within your enterprise data. You can use natural language or structured queries to find relevant answers, reveal insights, and enhance business processes with AI.
The IBM Watson® Discovery service is an installable cognitive search and content analytics engine that can be integrated into applications. It identifies patterns, trends, and actionable insights to support better decision-making. This service allows you to securely unify structured and unstructured data with pre-enriched content, using a simplified query language that eliminates the need for manual filtering of results.
Is it only for big business?
Sorry, but I do not know.

What is the cost of the service?

IBM Watson™ Discovery offers three plans: Lite, Advanced, and Premium. These plans provide varying levels of resources and capabilities to meet your needs. For subscription accounts, the monthly fee per instance is $500.

Ideally, find real-world user utterance examples that you can extract from existing business processes. The user examples should be tailored to your specific business. For example, if you are an insurance company, a user example might look more like this, I want to buy a new XYZ insurance plan.

The examples that you provide are used by your assistant to build a machine learning model that can recognize the same and similar types of utterances and map them to the appropriate intent.



Start with a few intents, and test them as you iteratively expand the scope of the application.

!

* There is no concept of an environment in v2. The deployment details such as size and index capacity are managed for you when you choose the appropriate service plan for your needs. For managed deployments, you can choose a Plus, Enterprise, or Premium plan, for example. For installed deployments, the sizing is managed by the deployment type that you specify when you install the service in Cloud Pak for Data.
* There is no single configuration object in v2. Control of the enrichments that are applied to documents is managed in the collections and project objects in v2. Other v1 configuration capabilities, such as the ability to customize the conversion step of ingestion, are not available in v2.

 What if I don't want to use managed services, but I want to install and manage my own software? 

Self-installed (or "bring your own") software from third parties is permitted without special approval. Examples include databases, logging stacks, web application firewalls, and so on. But just like first-party software you might develop and deploy, self-installed third-party software must comply with all of the requirements of the IBM Cloud Framework for Financial Services. And, it is your responsibility to provide appropriate supporting evidence.
